newsitem.title: NIGER: Low turnout in Niger poll as opposition boycotts.
newsitem.headline: Low turnout in Niger poll as opposition boycotts.

text.p: Voters in the West African nation of Niger cast their ballots for a new national assembly on Saturday with coupmaker-turned-president Ibrahim Bare Mainassara urging a huge turnout despite an opposition boycott.
But witnesses said turnout by midday was low, suggesting voters were following the opposition boycott call or just plain fed up with their third parliamentary poll in three years.

"I hope that the people of Niger will turn out massively to vote so we can extricate ourselves from this never-ending cycle of elections and devote ourselves to reviving the economy," the president said after voting in the capital Niamey's town hall.
Saturday's election was the sixth poll of any kind in this vast, poverty-stricken and mainly Moslem nation in four years.

Security was discrete initially despite a chaotic July presidential poll, which politicians accused Mainassara of rigging. Riot police later patrolled the capital. Two police helicopters flew overhead.

Polling began on time at 8 a.m. (0700 GMT) in Niamey and most towns. Witnesses reported slight delays in Diffa and Bilma in the north east. Voters flocked to vote in July around noon. Final turnout was 66.34 percent.

"In the towns, people are dragging their feet but we hope that the trend will turn around before the end of polling," a member of the electoral commission told state radio from Dosso 140 km (90 miles) east of Niamey on Saturday.

Opposition politicians, including Mahamane Ousmane, the elected civilian president Mainassara ousted in January, refused to register for Saturday's poll demanding that the result of the July presidential election be scrapped.
"I regret this because I had hoped that all Niger citizens would rally round a consensus to organise this poll," Mainassara said.

Negotiations between the two sides collapsed after repeated extensions of the registration date with the opposition Front for the Restoration and Defence of Democracy standing by its demands, which also included reinstatement of a scrapped independent electoral commission.

In July, Mainassara suspended the commission on the second day of polling, accusing it of irregularities, and placed his opponents under house arrest. He appointed a new commission which declared him winner with 52.22 percent of votes cast.
The United States said the election was fraudulent and suspended development aid.
A total of 220 candidates from around a dozen parties were running for the 83-seat assembly, including the Union of Independents for Democratic Renewal which supports Mainassara.
Around 3.8 million people were eligible to vote at more than 8,300 polling stations. Niger closed its borders for the poll.
Like many of its neighbours in sub-Saharan Africa, Niger launched democratic reforms in the 1990s after the collapse of Communist rule in the Soviet Union.
It held presidential parliamentary elections in 1993 but squabbling between Mahamane and his prime minister Amadou Hama from a rival party paralysed government.
Early parliamentary elections in January 1995 failed to resolve the standoff. Mainassara seized power a year later.
Polls close at 7 p.m. (1800 GMT). Provisional results, which the Supreme Court must verify, could be known within 48 hours.
